title: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles
summary: Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.
subject: History
unit: Road to revolution and the Revolution
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: Revolutionary War Battles
layers.shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words.

layers.name: Revolutionary War Battlefields
layers.shows: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Turning Points
layers.shows: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor.
layers.source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources

layers.name: Thirteen British Colonies
layers.shows: Colony areas and borders in 1763. The pop-up gives the colony's name.
layers.source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)

layers.name: 1763 Proclamation Line
layers.shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlement
layers.source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)

layers.name: Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781
layers.shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. The layer has no pop-ups and no labels.

knownIssues.where: Turning Points layer, circles 1 and 3 to 5
knownIssues.note: Circle 1 (Lexington and Concord) gives Victor: Britain; it was an American victory, as the Revolutionary War Battles legend shows. The layer's Notes field on circles 3 to 5 holds the next circle's text and is cut off mid-sentence; the pop-up shows the Battle_details field instead, which is correct. The MapMaker team is correcting the layer. Until then, use the Battle_details text in the pop-up and the Battles legend for the winner.

compellingQuestion.en: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Por qué los combates pasaron de Boston a Nueva York, y luego a través de Nueva Jersey, en 1775–1776?

questions.task: Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

student.en: Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord. When was it fought? Use the legend to find out who won. Then click the Boston diamond: how long did the siege of Boston last?
student.es: Abre el marcador Massachusetts. Haz clic en el rombo de Lexington and Concord. ¿Cuándo fue la batalla? Usa la leyenda para saber quién ganó. Luego haz clic en el rombo de Boston: ¿cuánto duró el sitio de Boston?

fill.en: Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia en línea recta de Boston a Concord: ________ millas

answer.where: Massachusetts bookmark. Lexington and Concord pop-up, the date line under the title: April 19, 1775. Legend (Revolutionary War Battles): blue diamond = American Victory, red = British Victory. Boston pop-up: April 19, 1775 to March 17, 1776, about 11 months. Measure tool, Boston to Concord: about 16 miles (accept 15 to 17).
answer.text: Use the Revolutionary War Battles legend for the result.

title.en: Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?
title.es: ¿Dónde se combatió en 1775 y dónde se combatió en 1776?

questions.task: Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

student.en: Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one and write its name under the year it was fought. Use the legend to mark who won. Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
student.es: Aléjate hasta ver todos los rombos, desde Quebec hasta Carolina del Sur. Haz clic en cada uno y escribe su nombre bajo el año en que se combatió. Usa la leyenda para marcar quién ganó. ¿Qué colonias tuvieron batallas en 1775? ¿Y en 1776? ¿Qué cambió?

answer.where: Revolutionary War Battles layer, zoomed out to the whole east coast: 21 diamonds. Each pop-up's date line gives the year; the diamond color and the legend give the winner. The colony comes from the Thirteen British Colonies layer or the pop-up's account.
answer.accept: A good answer lists most of the 21 battles under the right year (8 in 1775, 13 in 1776), names Massachusetts, New York, Virginia and Quebec for 1775 and adds North Carolina, South Carolina, New Jersey and Rhode Island for 1776, and says that the fighting began around Boston and then spread along the coast, with most battles from August 1776 in New York and New Jersey, where the British won nearly all of them.

questions.task: Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group). Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, name the major ports between Boston and Charleston (the layer has no pop-ups, so the battle diamonds and the coastline help), measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

student.en: In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (it's inside Revolutionary War Battlefields). Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port. Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? The layer has no pop-ups, so use the coastline and the battle diamonds nearby to name them. Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston. Looking at the map, what could a navy based at New York reach?
student.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (ciudades portuarias clave; está dentro de Revolutionary War Battlefields). Usa la leyenda para distinguir un puerto principal (Major Port City) de un puerto menor (Port). Boston y Charleston son puertos principales: ¿qué otros puertos principales hay entre ellos? La capa no tiene ventanas emergentes, así que usa la costa y los rombos de batallas cercanos para nombrarlos. Mide de Nueva York a Filadelfia y de Nueva York a Boston. Mirando el mapa, ¿qué podía alcanzar una armada con base en Nueva York?

fill.en: New York to Philadelphia: ________ miles. New York to Boston: ________ miles
fill.es: De Nueva York a Filadelfia: ________ millas. De Nueva York a Boston: ________ millas

answer.where: Key Port Cities layer, legend: larger symbol = Major Port City, smaller = Port. Five major ports: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk and Charleston, so the three between Boston and Charleston are New York, Philadelphia and Norfolk. The layer has no pop-ups or labels: New York sits by the Brooklyn diamond, Norfolk by the Great Bridge diamond, and Philadelphia is up the Delaware River south-west of Trenton. Measure tool: New York to Philadelphia about 80 miles (accept 75 to 85); New York to Boston about 190 miles (accept 180 to 200).
answer.accept: A good answer names at least New York and Philadelphia, gives both distances within range, and says that New York is in the middle of the coast, a day or two's sail from Boston, Philadelphia and the Chesapeake, with a deep harbor and the Hudson River leading north, so a navy there could reach the other big ports and cut New England off from the rest of the colonies.
answer.text: Accept Norfolk if a student works it out; it is the hardest to name without labels. Background for teachers: [Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/brooklyn).

questions.task: Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

student.en: Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear, then follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. When was each fought, and who won?
student.es: Acércate a la ciudad de Nueva York hasta que aparezcan los círculos numerados y sigue los círculos 4 y 5. Haz clic en los rombos de Fort Washington, Fort Lee y Trenton. ¿Cuándo se combatió cada batalla y quién ganó?

fill.en: Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia de la ciudad de Nueva York a Trenton: ________ millas

answer.where: Turning Points circles 4 (Fall of New York City, 1776, Victor: Britain) and 5 (Washington Strikes Back, 1776, Victor: United States); the pop-up's Battle details text tells the story of each. Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups: Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, and Fort Lee, November 20, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776, blue = American Victory. Measure tool, New York City to Trenton: about 52 miles (accept 48 to 56).

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos lugares del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

beforeYouStart.en: British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.
beforeYouStart.es: Soldados británicos salieron de Boston para apoderarse de las armas que los colonos habían guardado en Concord. Los combates que siguieron dieron inicio a la Revolución estadounidense. Durante los dos años siguientes, el ejército y la armada británicos y el nuevo Ejército Continental, dirigido por George Washington, lucharon por las ciudades, los ríos y los puertos de las colonias.

readingTheMap.en: Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups: the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.
readingTheMap.es: Los rombos marcan las batallas. La ventana emergente de una batalla da su nombre, sus fechas y su historia, pero no dice quién ganó: el color del rombo muestra al ganador, así que usa la leyenda. Cada rombo está en el lugar donde se suele situar la batalla, pero los combates ocuparon un área mayor: las zonas grises muestran el campo de batalla y las zonas rayadas, el núcleo, donde la lucha fue más intensa. Acércate para ver círculos blancos numerados: cinco momentos decisivos, numerados en el orden en que ocurrieron. La capa Key Port Cities (ciudades portuarias clave) no tiene ventanas emergentes: la leyenda distingue un puerto principal de uno menor.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre 1775–1776 que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Open the map and check it loads. Every layer is on except Key Port Cities, which students turn on for question 3. Download the student sheet. Share the map with the Google Classroom button (it shares the map only; attach the sheet separately). No account or login is needed. Sketches are not saved, so students who sketch should finish in one session or take a screenshot. Read the answers on the teacher page.

misconceptions.claim: The early war was fought in Massachusetts.
misconceptions.response: By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.

misconceptions.claim: The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.
misconceptions.response: Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.

misconceptions.claim: The Americans lost every battle in 1776.
misconceptions.response: The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

standards.text: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
